Ma mère ne me disait pas « je t'aime »,: My mother didn't say “I love you,” but she showed it in everything she did. I admired her brown hands, smooth and sturdy. I remember very clearly being six or seven years old and looking at her beautiful hands. As I grew up, those hands took on more meaning. Calm hands that never hit, and that moved with great care and attention.
Maman ne nous a jamais dit qu'elle était: Mom never told us she had gone to residential school. She would mention small things in passing, about the “sisters.” It seemed to be something out of the ordinary, but no one explained to us why. My mother married at 18 and moved to British Columbia, far from her childhood life.
Ce n’est que lorsqu'elle tressait nos ch: It was only when she braided our hair that the subject came up. Sitting on the floor in front of her, I would close my eyes and savour the slow, steady brushing. Thinking out loud, she would let fragments slip out; all I understood was that they were about the “sisters.”
Quand j'ai quitté la maison pour aller à: When I left home to go to university, she started saying “I love you” on the phone.
À mon retour après ma première année, el: When I came home after my first year, she braided my hair while we watched TV. There was a CBC miniseries about residential schools. I watched until the floatplane landed. “That didn't happen to you, did it?” I asked her.
Maman a verbalisé sa réponse, sans me re: Mom put her answer into words, without looking at me. She was thinking. Finally, in a neutral voice, she said yes. In the years that followed, the pieces gradually came together. It explained the silence… Not only about residential schools, but also the silence that reigned in our home. It was a quiet household. My mother never engaged in any intense exchange or heated debate, whatever it was about. During arguments, she would go downstairs to do laundry and cry, rather than say what she thought.
Ma mère avait été emmenée au pensionnat: My mother was taken to St. Joseph's residential school when she was seven. The “sisters” she spoke of were the Daughters of the Heart of Mary. They ran a residential school for girls at Spanish River, Ontario, which was operated in partnership with the Government of Canada. Together with the boys' school, it was the largest residential school in Ontario.
Ma mère ne rentrait à la maison que pour: My mother only came home for the holidays, even though home was just across the river. She spoke only Anishinaabemowin, and understood nothing of what was said to her. “I didn't know anything, not even that I had to put up my hand to go to the toilet. So I wet my seat, and I was beaten for it.”
Elle répond à mes questions maintenant,: She answers my questions now, on the eve of the first National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. She held back for more than sixty years, but she answers in a direct, composed way. In her own way. Articles, films and testimonies had told me more about residential schools than my own mother had. It was others who informed me. Thinking back on their stories, I ask whether there were older children who had been there longer and could act as interpreters. Two of my mother's cousins were in the same class as her. “But they could only help me if they were told to,” she says. “I didn't understand, and it has never left me,” she continues. “It was just... confusing. I never understood what was going on, and then the fear and confusion never went away.”
Mon plus jeune a huit ans. Il est dans l: My youngest is eight. He's in the next room, and I catch myself imitating my mother's calm, measured voice. I check again, hoping she attended a day school, even though I know she didn't. My mind doesn't want to picture her small self there, at night. “I stayed until Christmas, or until summer. Even though my house was just across the river.” It's the idea that my mother was alone that hurts me the most.
Gabor Maté explique que c'est la raison: Gabor Maté explains that this is why trauma forms, and not just the wound itself. “[Children] are traumatized because they are alone with their pain,” he says. To me, it rings so true in so many ways that it's unbearable.
Ma mère a toujours aimé que ses enfants: My mother has always liked having her children present and close. She raised four children and a grandchild. She understood why a protective eye was necessary.
À la veille de la première de cette tout: On the eve of this very first national day, my mother describes her abandonment. In the choice of words, more than in the tone, I understand. She didn't have that moment of rupture people talk about in books, when a child has grown up and realizes how much it hurts parents to leave their children.
« Mes parents croyaient en l'Église, au: “My parents believed in the Church, in the education system, and they took me there.” I've learned that survivors' lives change when they hear that it wasn't a choice, that they were forced. Maybe my mother never had that moment. I take a breath, and I say: “Mom. They were threatened with jail if they didn't cooperate, right?” Her voice changes, becoming a little lighter.
Elle le savait, non? Je me le demande. C: She knew that, didn't she? I wonder. It's not possible that she didn't know it was imposed. She must have known… and isn't that what she had felt? Residential schools were another way for the government to try to break up Indigenous families, and the churches were involved.
Je voulais une photo de ma mère pour ce: I wanted a photo of my mother for this story; the one I had in mind was a class photo from the Spanish River school.
« Je ne l’ai plus. Je l'ai déchirée. Un: “I don't have it anymore. I tore it up. One day, I was so angry at the Catholic Church that I tore it up,” she told me that evening. I raise my eyebrows over the phone; that's not like her. She repeated the sentence for emphasis, which isn't like her either. I smile a little, picturing the scene.

En tant que journaliste, je parle avec b: As a journalist, I talk with a lot of people. I learn something in every interview, whether it's a heartbreaking story of racism or a brilliant project. Sharing these stories has given me insight that sometimes gives me new bearings for talking to my mother. I wrote about language initiatives while I was taking my first Ojibwe class.
Ma mère semblait un peu distante, me dis: My mother seemed a bit distant, telling me “it's too hard to learn.” For decades, I bristled and withdrew at the slightest rejection. Now, I pause and try again. I tell Mom I'm taking the class with my sixteen-year-old son, that it's “our” time together and that it's fun. I passed on to her a teaching I received from a young, brilliant Sylix language teacher.
Un aîné a expliqué ce qui caractérise le: An Elder explained what characterizes hesitant older learners and silent speakers. They cannot speak out loud until their pain is healed. My mother relaxes when she hears this teaching, and her voice changes. I hear her nod, agree. That's when she tells me: “I only spoke the language until I was seven. And being hit every time I spoke it made things hard. It's there, but I can't put it into words.” For the past twenty years, I've wanted to ask her “why”? Why didn't she tell us?
Nous l'aurions comprise, nous nous serio: We would have understood her, we would have felt less frustrated when she detached from emotional things. Instead, I share what an Elder explained during a blanket exercise, on Klahoose territory. In the circle, I asked the question and he answered. We didn't talk about it because we didn't want our grandchildren to feel this pain, I was told. Mom acknowledges with a sound. One of the most devastating consequences was being silenced. I say “was,” because now, we talk about it. With each new account from my mother, my world shifts, rebalances. We have become closer. Mom makes a point of telling me this: “Let's be clear, there were others who lived through much worse than me in those places.” She wants me to know so that I won't wonder, but she does herself a disservice by minimizing the pain of her childhood. This isn't the time to ask her for more; I'll bring it up with her next time.
Malgré cette initiation à ce qu'on appel: Despite this initiation into what's called “education,” she values higher education. In her late thirties, she began working in health care, upgrading and staging her diplomas as she went. She earned her nursing diploma around the time she turned 50. Coming full circle, she returned to her home territory to work with Elders, in long-term care. My mother says this new National Day for Truth and Reconciliation doesn't change what happened. I understand why she feels that way. There is so much action to be taken, and none of us trusts these governments. My mother tells me about what hurt us. We communicate, and it makes us grow.
